A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching title, authors, research questions and core experiments. Their complete text, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and consolidation.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM-team experiments on three psychology tasks and five ML benchmarks, alongside team-size, adversarial and conversation-analysis results.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and reports additional full-information controls, alternative coordination protocols and automated prompt-optimization experiments.

M1.justification: Appendix A replaces v1's uniformly selected final answerer with majority voting over agents' post-discussion answers, using random tie-breaking. v4 also introduces GEPA selection of task-specific Reveal Expert prompts in place of manual ML prompt tuning. These change central output-generation and prompting procedures.

E1.justification: The same three psychology tasks and five ML benchmarks remain. However, v4 Appendix D adds an information-distribution scenario in which every team member receives identical complete expert information, extending coverage beyond the previous concentrated, distributed and no-information conditions.

E2.justification: v4 Tables 2 and 7 add evaluated comparisons with chain-of-thought plus majority voting, multi-agent debate following Du et al. (2024), and an opt-out protocol. Debate and opt-out are tested under both information conditions. v1's individual-agent and ALOC comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v4 changes the stated final-answer rule and adds all-expert controls and alternative interaction procedures. GEPA introduces optimization on 10-problem subsets with five iterations, or ten for NASA, while ML evaluation remains at 100 problems per benchmark. These are substantive reported design changes; the PDFs do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests whether communication noise explains underperformance by evaluating teams of four fully informed experts. Appendices F and G test sensitivity to coordination protocols and expert-revelation prompts. These address previously untested explanations for the central failure; the earlier team-size, adversarial and conversation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly describes ML results as averaged over two seeds in Table 2 and Appendix D. v4 removes that statement and describes individual accuracies as averaged over the two information-condition runs, leaving ML replication counts unstated. This changes reporting without establishing fewer runs. Existing psychology SEM and correlation-reporting practices remain.

E6.justification: ML team and ALOC results are revised throughout Table 2. For example, MMLU Pro ENM/RE accuracies are 85.0/89.0 in v1 and 86.0/86.0 in v4, with ALOC changing from 92.5 to 91.8. The reported ML gap range changes from 8.1–37.6% to 6.3–41.1%. v4 adds control, alternative-protocol and GEPA outcomes. These are revised-procedure results, not established same-setting performance gains; existing psychology and correlation results largely remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The relative synergy-gap formula, identification/leveraging decomposition and ALOC definition remain unchanged. Neither version adds mathematical theorems or proofs. Revisions to the philosophical grounding of conversation coding concern conceptual positioning rather than formal theory.

C1.justification: The central claims about failed expertise leveraging, team-size dilution and adversarial robustness remain. The headline ML underperformance range changes to 6.3–41.1%, and v4 extends the failure claim across alternative coordination protocols. These refine the scope and quantitative statement without replacing the central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 newly interprets the full-information control as isolating expertise asymmetry from communication noise. It interprets GEPA results as identifying deliberation rather than prompt phrasing as the bottleneck, including discussion of extreme-deference prompts suppressing useful interaction. The impact statement also adds concrete cost and high-stakes deployment implications. The limitation concerning untested alignment causality already existed in v1.

D1.justification: v4 adds context-management details, explicitly documents team selection before observing team results, supplies alternative-protocol descriptions and GEPA budgets/full prompts, and provides a repository link where v1 only asserted an open-source release. Some dated model identifiers previously visible in ML plots disappear during consolidation.

R1.justification: v4 adds GEPA, Davidson et al.'s collaboration-gap study and Li et al.'s distributed-information study. It replaces parts of the epistemological citation basis with Zagzebski and removes Grundmann, Lackey, and Eisikovits and Feldman. The established five-axis positioning against prior multi-agent research remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: The main narrative and much wording remain intact. v4 makes localized introduction and discussion revisions, separates the conclusion from limitations, rewrites the impact statement, and reorganizes the ML appendix around consolidated summaries. New experimental appendices expand the document without an extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v1's ten ML performance and weak-synergy figures are replaced by v4 Tables 5–6. Main Table 2 is transposed and expanded with protocol rows, and new tables display full-information and alternative-protocol results. Existing psychology, adversarial and correlation plots are retained with relocation and some caption corrections.

improvement.justification: The alternative-protocol tests, full-information control and GEPA experiments address weaknesses in v1's reliance on one discussion procedure and manual prompt tuning. Added implementation details, prompts and consolidated tables improve auditability. However, v4 drops explicit ML seed reporting and introduces a reporting inconsistency: Section 3.3 says answer correctness is not revealed, while an Appendix G prompt declares the expert's initial answer known to be correct. The additions provide a net improvement, but these unresolved issues limit its strength.
